title: 📘 UNIT 4: THE MIDDLE AGES AND EARLY MODERN WORLD, C. 500 AD–1789
notes:
The unit covers two major periods of world history:

🏰 Middle Ages → about 500–1500 A.D., following the decline of the ancient world and preceding the development of early capitalist relations.

🌍 Early Modern World → about 1500–1789, ending with the beginning of the French Revolution.

Major historical themes → fall of the Western Roman Empire + Byzantine civilization + feudalism + revival of trade and towns + Crusades + Islamic civilization + Ottoman expansion + medieval China + early capitalism + European exploration + globalization + Renaissance + Reformation + Scientific Revolution + Enlightenment.

title: 4.1 🏰 The European Middle Ages
notes:
The European Middle Ages developed after the collapse of the Western Roman Empire.

Major themes → fall of Rome + Germanic invasions + Byzantine Empire + feudalism + manorialism + Christian Church + revival of towns and trade + Crusades + medieval culture and education.

📌 The period was formerly called the 'Dark Age', but historians now emphasize that medieval civilization developed through the blending of Greco-Roman, Germanic and Christian traditions.

title: 4.1.1 ⚔️ Fall of the Western Roman Empire and Dawn of the Middle Ages
notes:
The Western Roman Empire declined gradually because of:

• Internal problems.
• Separation from the wealthier Eastern Empire in 395 A.D.
• Invasions by Germanic peoples.
• Pressure from the Huns.
• Weakening of Roman military power.
• Disruption of trade.

Germanic peoples → originally came from Scandinavia and moved into central Europe. Some adopted Roman farming, Christianity and trade, while many remained organized in tribes under chiefs.

Important migrations/invasions:
• Visigoths → invaded Spain around 416 A.D.
• Angles, Jutes and Saxons → settled in Britain around 450 A.D.
• Franks → established a kingdom in Gaul in the 480s.
• Ostrogoths → invaded Italy.

476 A.D. → Rome fell to Germanic tribes, marking the conventional beginning of the European Middle Ages.

title: 4.1.1.1 🏛️ Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire
notes:
330 A.D. → Constantine the Great moved the Roman capital from Rome to Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople.

395 A.D. → Roman Empire was practically divided into Western and Eastern parts.

Byzantine Empire → name used for the Eastern Roman Empire.

476 A.D. → Western Roman Empire collapsed, while the Eastern Empire survived for about another 1,000 years.

Reasons for Byzantine survival → stronger economy + larger population + fortified cities + less exposure to Germanic invasions.

👑 Emperor → absolute ruler and chief lawmaker.

👸 Empress Theodora → wife, advisor and co-ruler of Justinian; actively participated in government affairs.

👑 Justinian I (527–565) → Byzantine Empire reached its greatest size; conquered Italy, part of Spain and North Africa while controlling Asia Minor, Balkans, Egypt, Palestine and Syria.

title: 4.1.1.1 📜 Byzantine Achievements and Culture
notes:
📜 Justinian Code → collection and organization of ancient Roman laws; later influenced legal systems in many countries.

⛪ Hagia Sophia → built by Justinian between 532–537 A.D.; largest and most splendid Christian church in Constantinople.

Economic life → most people were farmers producing grapes, olives and wheat or raising sheep; merchants and craftsmen worked in towns and cities.

Trade → imported silk, spices and luxury goods from China.

Cultural achievements:
• Preserved ancient Greek literature and philosophy.
• Preserved Roman governmental and legal traditions.
• Developed Byzantine art, music and architecture.
• Christianity became the official state religion.
• Missionaries spread Orthodox Christianity to Russians and other Slavic peoples.
• Greek church services and the Bible were translated into Old Slavonic.
• Cyrillic alphabet was developed for Slavic languages.

title: 4.1.1.1 ✝️ Byzantine Church Division and Decline
notes:
1054 A.D. → Christian Church divided into:
• Western Roman Catholic Church.
• Eastern Greek/Russian Orthodox Church.

Main dispute → authority of the Pope over the Eastern Church.

After Justinian's death → Byzantine Empire faced Germanic attacks and Persian invasions.

👑 Heraclius (610–642) → defeated the Persians during wars of 624–626.

7th century → Byzantines lost large territories to Arab expansion.

1071 → Seljuk Turks defeated Byzantine forces at the Battle of Manzikert, beginning the decline of Byzantine control in Asia Minor.

1095 → Emperor Alexius I asked Western European Christians for help against the Turks.

1453 → Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople; Byzantine Empire collapsed.

👑 Constantine XI → last Byzantine emperor, died defending Constantinople.

title: 4.1.1.2 🛡️ Western Europe During the Middle Ages
notes:
After Rome's fall, Western Europe experienced:
• Political division.
• Ruralization.
• Economic decline.
• Disrupted trade.
• Abandoned towns.
• Invasions.
• Decline of classical culture.

The period was once called the 'Dark Age', but medieval civilization gradually developed through the blending of:
→ Greco-Roman traditions + Germanic traditions + Christianity.

Major achievements of medieval Europe → Christianity became dominant + universities were founded + modern European states began developing + present-day European languages developed.

title: 4.1.1.2 👑 Frankish and Carolingian Kingdoms
notes:
Germanic kingdoms included:
• Ostrogoths → Italy.
• Visigoths → Spain.
• Franks → Gaul.
• Burgundians → western Germany.
• Saxons → England.

👑 Charles Martel → founded/consolidated the Carolingian dynasty.

732 A.D. → defeated Muslim Arab forces from Spain at the Battle of Tours, preventing further Muslim advance into Western Europe.

👑 Charlemagne (768–814) → grandson of Charles Martel; reunited much of the former Western Roman Empire.

His empire included → present-day France + Germany + part of Italy.

Achievements → strong central administration modeled on Rome + military expansion + revival of Latin learning + local schools + spread of Christian civilization.

800 A.D. → Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans.

843 A.D. → Carolingian Empire divided into three independent kingdoms after struggles among successors.

title: 4.2 🏰 Main Features of the Middle Ages
notes:
The major features of medieval Europe included:

🏰 Feudalism → political and social system based on landholding, loyalty and military service.

🌾 Manorialism → rural economic system centered on the manor.

⚔️ Knights → mounted warriors who served lords in return for land.

✝️ Church → major political, social, educational and cultural institution.

🏘️ Towns → revived as trade expanded.

🛍️ Guilds → organizations of merchants and craftsmen.

🎓 Universities → developed especially from the 12th century.

⚔️ Crusades → Christian military expeditions to the Holy Land.

💰 Revival of trade → weakened manorialism and encouraged money economy.

title: 4.2.1 🌾 Feudalism and Manorialism
notes:
Feudalism → loosely organized system in which powerful lords divided land among lesser lords in exchange for loyalty and service.

Vassal → lesser lord who received a fief from a greater lord in return for allegiance and military service.

Fief → plot of land granted to a vassal.

Vassalage → relationship linking kings, great lords and lesser lords.

Manor → lord's estate and the center of medieval rural economy.

Manorialism → self-sufficient rural economic system where the manor produced most of what its people needed.

Demesne → part of the manor directly controlled by the lord and cultivated through compulsory serf labour.

Serfs → peasants tied to the manor who could not leave without the lord's permission.

Serfs paid → labour services + agricultural products + cash + fees for using mills, ovens and presses.

In return → they received land to cultivate and protection from warfare and raids.

title: 4.2.2 👑 Medieval Social Hierarchy
notes:
Medieval feudal society was divided into privileged and unprivileged groups.

👑 King → highest political authority.

🏰 Nobles/Lords → received fiefs and exercised local government, taxation, justice and military power.

⚔️ Knights → mounted warriors who received land for military service.

✝️ Higher clergy → bishops and other senior church officials, often from noble families.

🌾 Peasants/Serfs → largest and lowest social group; performed labour and paid dues.

📌 Social position was largely determined by birth.

📌 Vassalage was generally hereditary, while serfs had very limited social mobility.

title: 4.2.3 ⚔️ Knights and Chivalry
notes:
Knights → heavily armed mounted warriors who fought for kings and great lords.

Their equipment → horse + armour + shield + lance + sword.

In return for military service → knights received land that supported their horses, armour and weapons.

Chivalry → code of conduct adopted by knights especially during the Late Middle Ages (1350–1500).

Chivalry required knights to be:
• Brave.
• Loyal.
• Truthful.
• Fair in warfare.
• Respectful toward captured knights.

📌 Captured knights could sometimes be released after promising to pay ransom.

title: 4.2.4 👩 Women in Medieval Society
notes:
Noble women could manage estates when husbands or fathers were away at war.

Responsibilities → supervising vassals + managing households + agricultural activities + medical tasks + sometimes defending estates.

Some noble women participated actively in politics, especially during the High and Late Middle Ages.

Inheritance → women's rights were restricted; land normally passed to the eldest son.

📌 Women could sometimes inherit fiefs or receive land as dowry.

title: 4.2.5 ✝️ Church and Medieval Europe
notes:
The Christian Church became one of the most powerful institutions of medieval Europe.

Europe was often called → Christendom.

Church functions → government services + taxation + law and order + education + hospitals + care for travelers.

11th century → Church became stronger and more independent.

1059 → College of Cardinals was created to elect the Pope.

👤 Pope Innocent III (1198–1216) → claimed that papal authority was above that of other rulers.

The Church became the largest landholder in Western Europe.

📌 Bishops and high clergy often controlled large fiefs and lived similarly to nobles.

title: 4.2.6 🏘️ Revival of Trade and Towns
notes:
From the 11th century → trade began to revive and towns expanded.

Reasons for town growth → increased demand for goods + major trade routes + fortified castles + churches/monasteries + natural resources.

People moved to towns seeking employment and better opportunities.

Town occupations → weaving + shoemaking + baking + butchery + carpentry + trading + other crafts.

By about 1000 A.D. → merchants, traders and artisans formed a new middle class between nobles and peasants.

📌 Growing trade weakened the manorial system and encouraged a money economy.

title: 4.2.7 🛠️ Guild System
notes:
Guild → organized association of merchants or craftsmen with common economic interests.

Merchant guilds → appeared first.

Craft guilds → later formed by artisans in particular occupations.

Examples → weavers + bakers + goldsmiths.

Functions of guilds:
• Protected economic interests.
• Controlled quality of products.
• Regulated working hours.
• Set prices.
• Organized workers within occupations.

👩 Women → participated in crafts and trade; some inherited workshops and in some places formed or dominated guilds.

📌 Guilds became an important part of medieval urban economic life.

title: 4.2.8 🎨 Medieval Art, Architecture and Education
notes:
Town life encouraged art, learning and intellectual activity.

Two major achievements → construction of cathedrals + growth of universities.

🏛️ Romanesque architecture → massive walls + strong columns + rounded arches.

🏰 Gothic architecture → high towers + pointed arches + flying buttresses.

Cathedral art → wood carving + stone sculpture + stained glass + religious images.

🎓 Medieval education → largely controlled by the Church.

Monastery and cathedral schools taught:
• Church music.
• Theology.
• Latin.
• Grammar.
• Rhetoric.
• Logic.
• Arithmetic.
• Geometry.
• Astronomy.
• Harmonics.

These subjects were known as the Seven Liberal Arts.

title: 4.2.9 🎓 Medieval Universities
notes:
The first modern European universities developed during the 1100s.

Universities initially developed as associations or guilds of scholars rather than large collections of buildings.

📍 University of Paris → became one of the largest and most famous universities in Europe during the 13th century and served as a model for northern European universities.

Teaching language → Latin.

Many universities developed from teachers' guilds connected with cathedral schools.

Teachers' guilds → charged fees for teaching and granting degrees.

📌 The growth of universities contributed to the revival of learning in Europe.

title: 4.2.10 ✝️ Crusades, 1096–1270
notes:
Crusades → successive military expeditions organized mainly by Western European Christians to recapture the Holy Land/Palestine.

Holy Land → important to Christians because Jesus Christ lived there.

Background → Seljuk Turks conquered Asia Minor, Palestine and Syria and defeated the Byzantine army at Manzikert in 1071.

1095 → Byzantine Emperor Alexius I asked Western Christians for military assistance.

👤 Pope Urban II → called for a Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095.

1096 → large numbers of knights and ordinary people began travelling to the Holy Land.

Crux → Latin word for cross; Crusaders wore the cross symbol on their clothing.

title: 4.2.10.1 ⚔️ Major Crusades and Motives
notes:
Eight major expeditions occurred between 1096 and 1270:

1️⃣ 1096–1099
2️⃣ 1147–1149
3️⃣ 1189–1192
4️⃣ 1202–1204
5️⃣ 1217–1221
6️⃣ 1228–1229
7️⃣ 1248–1254
8️⃣ 1270

Stated goals → permanent control of the Holy Land + protection of the Byzantine Empire.

Other motives:
• French knights wanted land and wealth.
• Italian merchants wanted access to Middle Eastern trade.
• Pope wanted greater authority and church unity.
• Priests and monks sought religious relics.
• Poor people sought escape from hardship.

📌 Religious motivation was important, but economic, political and social motives also influenced participation.

title: 4.2.10.2 🕌 Results and Impacts of the Crusades
notes:
1099 → First Crusade captured Jerusalem.

1187 → Salah al-Din (Saladin) recaptured Jerusalem.

Third Crusade → led by Frederick I Barbarossa, Richard I of England and Philip II of France; failed to retake Jerusalem.

Salah al-Din later allowed Christian pilgrims to visit the Holy City.

1204 → Fourth Crusade attacked fellow Christians, captured and looted Constantinople.

Major impacts:
• Increased Mediterranean trade.
• Improved European shipbuilding.
• Increased use of money economy.
• Weakened serfdom.
• Increased monarchs' revenues and prestige.
• Increased papal power.
• Improved maps and navigation.
• Increased European curiosity about Asia.
• Encouraged wider European contacts.
• Contributed to development of early capitalist relations.

title: 4.3 🌏 The Middle Ages in Asia
notes:
Major themes in medieval Asia → rise and expansion of Islam + Islamic civilization + Ottoman expansion + Chinese dynasties + Tang and Song achievements + Mandate of Heaven.

Major Islamic centers → Baghdad + Cairo + Cordoba + Timbuktu.

Major Chinese dynasties discussed → Sui + Tang + Song + Yuan + Ming + Qing.

title: 4.3.1 ☪️ Rise and Expansion of Islam
notes:
Islam → religion preached in Arabia by Prophet Muhammad in the 7th century A.D.

👤 Muhammad → born in Mecca around 570 A.D.; preached belief in one God, Allah, and that Muhammad was His messenger.

Islam → submission to the will of Allah.

Quran → holy scripture of Islam.

610 A.D. → Muhammad began preaching in Mecca.

Quraysh merchants → opposed Muhammad because his teachings threatened their privileges and Mecca's traditional religious and economic importance.

622 A.D. → Muhammad and followers migrated from Mecca to Yathrib, later called Medina.

Hijra/Hijira → migration to Medina; beginning of the Islamic calendar.

Ansars → inhabitants of Medina who helped Muhammad's followers.

Muhajirun → emigrants who migrated with Muhammad.

Sahaba → companions of the Prophet.

Umma → Muslim community.

title: 4.3.1.1 🕋 Muhammad and the Early Caliphate
notes:
630 A.D. → Muhammad entered Mecca victoriously and rededicated the Ka'aba to Allah.

He then worked to unite Arabia under Islam through diplomacy and warfare.

632 A.D. → Muhammad died.

First four caliphs:
👤 Abu Bakr → 632–634.
👤 Umar → 634–644.
👤 Uthman → 644–656.
👤 Ali → 656–661.

After Uthman's murder → Ali became caliph, but Muawiya and others rejected his leadership.

This produced civil war and eventually contributed to the division of Muslims into major sectarian traditions.

title: 4.3.1.2 ☪️ Sunni, Shi'ite and Kharijite Islam
notes:
🟢 Sunni → believed a qualified pious Muslim from Muhammad's tribe could lead the community; followed the Sunna, the way of the Prophet.

🔵 Shi'ite → believed Muhammad had designated Ali as successor; emphasized the Imamate and the authority of the Imam.

🔴 Kharijites → withdrew from Ali's followers after the arbitration; believed leadership could belong to any qualified, pious Muslim regardless of social origin.

📌 Sunni legal sources → Quran + Hadith + community consensus + analogy.

📌 Shi'ite legal sources → Quran + Hadith of Prophet and Imams + consensus of Imams + reason.

Major Sunni schools → Hanafi + Maliki + Shafi + Hanbali.

Major Shi'a schools → Zaydi + Ja'fari.

📍 Ethiopia → Shafi and Hanafi schools are dominant according to the textbook.

title: 4.3.1.3 📖 Sharia and Islamic Society
notes:
Sharia → body of Islamic law based on interpretation of the Quran, examples from Muhammad's life and Muslim traditions.

Functions → guides religious principles + legal matters + individual behaviour + community life.

Islamic civilization emphasized:
• Spiritual equality of Muslims.
• Rights and protection of women.
• Education for men and women.
• Study of the Quran.

📌 Different schools of fiqh developed from different interpretations of Islamic law during the 8th and 9th centuries.

title: 4.3.1.4 🕌 Rise of the Islamic Empire
notes:
Under the first four caliphs → Muslim Arabs expanded beyond Arabia.

Major conquests:
• Syria and Palestine → 634–636.
• Jerusalem → captured during the same campaigns.
• Egypt → 639–642.
• Iraq → Battle of Qadisiyya, 637.
• Persian Empire → defeated after Battle of Nihawand, 642.

By 650 A.D. → Muslim armies reached India, northern Iraq and Armenia.

Reasons for rapid expansion:
• Exhaustion of Byzantine and Persian empires.
• Harsh taxation by Byzantines.
• Religious tensions in Persia.
• Persian dynastic conflicts.
• Unity created by Islam.
• Desire to spread and strengthen the new religion.

title: 4.3.1.5 🏛️ Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates
notes:
👑 Muawiya → founded the Umayyad Caliphate in 661 A.D.

Umayyad Caliphate → 661–750.
Capital → Damascus.

Umayyad expansion → Central Asia + Sindh in India + North Africa + Sicily + Spain.

711 A.D. → Umayyads invaded Spain.

👑 Abu al-Abbas → leader of Abbasid revolution.

750 A.D. → Abbasids defeated the Umayyads and established their capital at Baghdad.

Abbasid Caliphate → 750–1258.

Early Abbasids → reduced Arab military privilege + ended discrimination against non-Arab Muslims + encouraged science and culture.

By 820 A.D. → Abbasid power was extensive.

By 920 A.D. → caliph's political power had weakened.

title: 4.3.1.6 📉 Decline of the Abbasid Caliphate
notes:
Internal factors:
• Exploitation and heavy taxation.
• Rebellions.
• Civil wars.
• Religious and clan conflicts.
• Fragmentation of provincial control.

Independent dynasties appeared in → Egypt + Persia + Tunisia + Maghreb + Spain.

External factors:
• Expansion of Seljuk Turks.
• Seljuk control over Baghdad.
• Mongol expansion.

1258 A.D. → Mongol forces led by Hulagu captured and destroyed Baghdad and killed the last Abbasid caliph.

📌 Fall of Baghdad → marked the end of the Abbasid Caliphate.

title: 4.3.1.7 🧠 Legacy of Muslim Civilization
notes:
Islamic Golden Age → approximately 800–1200 A.D.

Muslim civilization absorbed and developed knowledge from:
• Greeks.
• Persians.
• Hindus.
• Egyptians.
• Jews.
• Turks.
• Berbers.
• Spaniards.

Economic achievements → extensive trade network + money economy + irrigation + agricultural improvement.

Crops → dates + grain + sugar cane + cotton + medicinal herbs + flowers.

Trade connected → settled farmers and desert nomads.

📌 Muslim merchants spread products, technologies, knowledge and culture across a huge region.

title: 4.3.1.8 🔬 Muslim Advances in Science and Learning
notes:
Major fields of advancement:
• Mathematics.
• Astronomy.
• Botany.
• Chemistry.
• Medicine.
• Geography.
• History.
• Philosophy.

Major centers → Baghdad + Cairo + Cordoba + Timbuktu.

Muslim scholars translated → Greek + Persian + Sanskrit + other ancient works into Arabic.

Mathematics → algebra + trigonometry + geometry + decimal fractions; Hindu-Arabic numerals were transmitted to Europe.

🏦 Banking → banks existed in Baghdad and other cities by the 9th century.

🏥 Medicine → hospitals were established and physicians travelled to rural areas.

👤 Ibn Sina (Avicenna) → wrote Canon on Medicine, used as a European medical textbook for centuries.

👤 Muhammad al-Razi → major physician who wrote extensively on medicine and studied smallpox and measles.

👤 Hunayn ibn Ishaq → important work in optics.

🔭 Astronomy → use of astrolabes + astronomical observation + development of instruments.

👤 Ibn Khaldun → emphasized economic and social causes of historical events and warned historians against bias, exaggeration and unreliable sources.

title: 4.3.1.9 🕌 Islamic Art, Architecture and Literature
notes:
Muslim architecture → domed mosques + arches + high minarets.

Other buildings → palaces + schools + public buildings.

Art → manuscript illustration + abstract designs + highly developed calligraphy.

📚 Literature and scholarship → Arabic became a major language of government, science and literature.

📌 Muslim scholars preserved and expanded ancient knowledge, helping transmit Greek, Persian and Hindu learning to later civilizations.

title: 4.3.2 🕌 Expansion of the Ottoman Turkish Empire
notes:
Ottomans → Turkish-speaking pastoralists who migrated from Central Asia.

They converted to Sunni Islam and later became a major Muslim power.

👑 Osman/Othman I (1299–1324) → founder of the Ottoman state and dynasty.

From around 1280 → Ottoman expansion across Asia Minor and the Balkans.

Military advantage → effective use of cannons and muskets.

1453 → Sultan Mehmet II conquered Constantinople.

Constantinople → renamed Istanbul and became Ottoman capital.

Ottoman expansion later included → Iraq + Syria + Palestine + Arabian Peninsula + Egypt + Cyprus + Crete + parts of southern Ukraine and Poland + most of Hungary.

👑 Suleiman I (1520–1566) → Ottoman power reached its height; known as 'the Lawgiver' by his people and 'the Magnificent' by Europeans.

title: 4.3.2.1 🏛️ Ottoman Society and Administration
notes:
Ottoman society was divided into major social groups:

1️⃣ Soldiers and state officials → mostly Muslims; included lawyers, judges and poets.
2️⃣ Merchants, tax collectors and artisans.
3️⃣ Farmers and herders → included many non-Muslims.

Millets → religious communities organized according to faith, including Muslims, Greek Christians, Armenian Christians and Jews.

Millet leaders → responsible for education and some legal affairs within their communities.

👑 Sultan → absolute ruler.

Grand Vizier → chief minister and sometimes commander of the army.

Ulema → Muslim religious scholars whose interpretation of Sharia limited the Sultan's authority in religious/legal matters.

title: 4.3.2.2 ⚔️ Ottoman Military System
notes:
Janissaries → professional elite infantry and core of the Ottoman army.

Recruitment → Christian boys from the Balkans were taken as tribute, converted to Islam and trained as soldiers.

Janissaries → disciplined + highly trained + equipped with muskets and cannons.

Sipahi → Turkish cavalry.

Timar → landholding/fief granted to Sipahi by the Sultan.

Timar system → similar in some ways to European feudal fiefs.

📌 Ottoman military strength came from disciplined infantry + cavalry + firearms + strong administration + navy.

title: 4.3.2.3 📉 Decline of the Ottoman Empire
notes:
After the death of Suleiman I in 1566 → Ottoman decline gradually began.

Major factors:
• Economic decline from the 17th century.
• Military decline.
• European advances in commerce.
• European advances in military technology.
• Austrian expansion.
• Russian expansion.

📌 By the 18th century → European states increasingly captured Ottoman territories and pushed the empire backward.

title: 4.3.3 🇨🇳 Dynastic Cycle in China
notes:
Mandate of Heaven → belief that Heaven granted a ruler the right to govern China.

Dynastic Cycle → pattern in which a dynasty rises, achieves prosperity, becomes corrupt, loses the Mandate of Heaven and eventually falls.

Typical cycle:

🟢 New dynasty → brings peace + rebuilds infrastructure + gives land to peasants + protects people.

🔴 Old dynasty → overtaxes people + stops protecting them + allows infrastructure to decay + treats people unfairly.

⚠️ Problems → floods + earthquakes + peasant revolts + invasions + bandit attacks.

📌 A new ruler then claims the Mandate of Heaven and establishes a new dynasty.

The idea of the dynastic cycle continued until the end of imperial rule in China in 1912.

title: 4.3.3.1 🏯 Sui and Tang Dynasties
notes:
🏯 Sui Dynasty (581–618)

After nearly 400 years of division → Sui rulers reunited northern and southern China.

605 A.D. → Grand Canal rebuilt, connecting the Yangtze region with northern China.

Grand Canal → transported grain and products from the south to support political and military needs of the north.

🏯 Tang Dynasty (618–907)

First emperor → Li Yuan (618–626).

Tang period → prosperity + territorial expansion + cultural achievements.

Capital → Chang'an, one of the world's largest cities.

Major cultural figures → Li Po/Li Bao + Du Fu.

Religion → Buddhism strongly influenced culture; Confucianism revived in the 9th century.

Government → restored Han administrative system + expanded civil service based on talent + promoted education + redistributed land.

👸 Empress Wu Zhao (690–705) → only Chinese woman to declare herself 'Son of Heaven'.

Tang decline → rebellions + loss of Central Asian territories + corruption + drought + famine.

907 A.D. → Tang dynasty ended.

title: 4.3.3.2 🏯 Song Dynasty
notes:
960 A.D. → Song Dynasty reunified China.

Song Dynasty → 960–1279.

Achievements:
• Completed the civil service system.
• Introduced Neo-Confucianism as state philosophy.
• Improved farming methods.
• Expanded commerce.
• Encouraged learning and arts.
• Expanded foreign trade.

Foreign merchants → came from India, Persia and Arabia.

Trade reached → Southeast Asia for spices and special woods.

Major Chinese inventions associated with the Song period:
🧨 Gunpowder.
🧭 Magnetic compass.
🖨️ Movable-type printing.

📌 Art, philosophy and literature also flourished.

title: 4.3.3.3 🐎 Yuan, Ming and Qing Dynasties
notes:
🏹 Yuan Dynasty (1279–1368)

Mongol conquest → completed in 1279.

👑 Kublai Khan → grandson of Genghis Khan; established Yuan rule over China.

Capital → Khanbaliq (Beijing).

Mongols → upper ruling class; Chinese officials filled many lower administrative positions.

👤 Marco Polo → visited Kublai Khan's court and later described China's wealth and civilization.

📌 Mongol protection expanded Eurasian trade and helped spread Chinese products such as gunpowder, porcelain, paper and playing cards.

🏯 Ming Dynasty (1368–1644)
→ expelled Mongols + restored Chinese rule + restored civil service and Confucian learning + encouraged literature and art + conducted naval expeditions to Southeast Asia, India, Red Sea and East Africa.

🏯 Qing/Ching Dynasty (1644–1912)
→ established by Manchu rulers from Manchuria.
→ initially faced legitimacy problems but gained acceptance through strong government, suppression of rebellions and support for Chinese culture.
→ declined from the mid-19th century because of peasant revolts and Western pressure.

title: 4.4 💰 Development of Early Capitalism: 1500–1789
notes:
Capitalist relations developed gradually during the Late Middle Ages and expanded more rapidly after 1500.

14th century problems → war + plague + peasant rebellions + economic disruption.

Hundred Years' War (1337–1453) → conflict between England and France that disrupted trade and weakened economies.

Black Death (1347–1352) → plague epidemic that killed about one-fourth of Europe's population.

Other problems → drought + floods + famine.

Economic revival → began during the second half of the 15th century.

New urban groups → merchants + shopkeepers + bankers + professionals.

They accumulated capital for investment, encouraging development of financial institutions and banks.

📌 Legal equality of citizens, however, did not become widespread in most of Europe until after the French Revolution of 1789.

title: 4.4.1 🏘️ Development of Towns and Long-Distance Trade
notes:
c.1000–1300 → towns and cities grew rapidly and long-distance trade expanded.

Towns became centers of:
• Markets.
• Craft production.
• Manufacturing workshops.
• Long-distance trade.
• Administration.
• Religion.
• Culture.
• Education.

Countryside → supplied food to towns.

Towns → supplied manufactured goods to the countryside.

Merchant guilds → organized merchants and controlled trade.

Craft workers → often became wage workers under merchant capitalists.

Italian cities → especially Venice and Genoa, became major centers of Mediterranean trade.

📌 Luxury goods such as silk and spices were highly profitable.

title: 4.4.2 🏦 Money Economy, Banks and Bourgeoisie
notes:
As towns became wealthier → money economy expanded.

Banks → appeared especially in Italian cities.

Rich merchants → lent money at interest and financed trade through agents across Europe.

Bourgeoisie → wealthy urban citizens, especially merchants, who increasingly controlled town administration and commerce.

Some cities gained self-government by:
• Paying feudal lords/bishops/kings.
• Struggling for political rights.

Venice → developed into an independent city republic.

German free cities → managed their own affairs with limited outside control.

📌 There was no serfdom in medieval towns; the saying 'City air is free air' reflected this freedom.

title: 4.5 🧭 Age of Exploration and Inception of Globalization
notes:
Age of Exploration → began in the 15th century and continued into the early 17th century.

Main purpose → search for new trade routes + wealth + knowledge.

European demand → jewels + porcelain + silk + cinnamon + cloves + pepper + other Asian goods.

Problem → Ottoman Turks controlled important land and sea routes and charged high prices.

Therefore → Portugal and Spain sought alternative sea routes to Asia.

Other motivations:
• Curiosity about distant lands.
• Stories of wealth from Marco Polo.
• Legend of Prester John.
• Desire for gold.
• Religious motives.
• Political competition.

Technology → improved sailing ships + compass + quadrant + astrolabe + knowledge of seasonal winds made long-distance voyages possible.

title: 4.5.1 🚢 Portuguese Exploration
notes:
👑 Prince Henry the Navigator (1394–1460) → encouraged Portuguese exploration along the African coast.

His goals → expand Portuguese trade + find the source of West African gold.

He supported:
• Training sailors.
• Better ships.
• Mapmaking.
• Astronomy.
• Mathematics.
• Navigation.

Portuguese sailors → explored West African islands and eventually reached the southern tip of Africa.

Cape of Good Hope → name given to southern tip of Africa.

👤 Vasco da Gama → 1497–1498 sailed around the Cape of Good Hope to India.

📌 Vasco da Gama opened the sea route around Africa and across the Indian Ocean to Asia.

title: 4.5.2 🇪🇸 Spanish Exploration and the Americas
notes:
Spain also sought new routes to Asia.

👤 Christopher Columbus → Italian explorer working for Spain.

1492 → first voyage across the Atlantic while attempting to reach Asia.

Instead → reached the West Indies and coastal regions of the Americas.

📌 His voyages opened the way for Spanish conquest and colonization of the Americas.

👤 Hernán Cortés → destroyed the Aztec Empire of Mexico.

👤 Francisco Pizarro → destroyed the Inca Empire of Peru.

Portugal → established Brazil after Pedro Álvares Cabral's voyage in 1500.

👤 Ferdinand Magellan → 1519–1522 expedition became the first voyage to sail around the world.

Magellan → killed in the Philippines in 1521.

Victoria → only one of the original five ships to return to Spain in 1522.

title: 4.5.3 🌍 Northern European Exploration and Colonization
notes:
15th–16th centuries → Portugal and Spain led European exploration.

17th–18th centuries → Dutch, French and British increasingly took the lead.

👤 John Cabot → reached what is believed to be Newfoundland in 1497.

👤 Giovanni da Verrazano → reached the entrance of the Hudson River in 1524.

👤 Henry Hudson → mapped Manhattan in 1609.

English → established Jamestown in 1607.

French → Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec City in 1608.

Dutch → established New Amsterdam in 1624.

Plantation colonies → developed in Brazil, Caribbean and parts of North America and relied heavily on slave labour.

📌 Global trade expanded rapidly, producing the Commercial Revolution.

title: 4.5.4 🔄 Commercial Expansion and Global Trade
notes:
Portugal → focused strongly on trading posts in Africa and Asia and controlled much Far Eastern trade during the 16th century.

1580 → Portugal was annexed by Spain for about 60 years.

Dutch → gained many former Portuguese trading possessions and controlled the Dutch East Indies.

British East India Company → controlled much of India's trade; British control was nearly complete by 1763.

French → maintained some trading posts in India.

📌 European exploration created an increasingly connected network of communication, trade and colonies.

📌 Exploration did not completely stop; Australia, Arctic, Antarctic and the interior of Africa remained partly unexplored by Europeans for much longer.

title: 4.5.5 🌽 Columbian Exchange
notes:
Columbian Exchange → exchange of plants, animals and diseases between the Old World and New World after European contact with the Americas.

🌎 Americas → Europe/Africa/Asia:
• Maize.
• Potatoes.
• Sweet potatoes.
• Cassava.
• Tomatoes.
• Pumpkins.
• Chili peppers.
• Cacao.
• Peanuts.
• Pineapple.

🌍 Old World → Americas:
• Wheat.
• Grapes.
• Bananas.
• Sugar cane.
• Coffee.
• Horses.
• Donkeys.
• Cattle.
• Pigs.
• Goats.
• Chickens.

Diseases also crossed the Atlantic → measles + smallpox affected Native Americans severely; syphilis spread in Europe.

Major effects → population growth from new food crops + migration of millions of Europeans to the Americas.

title: 4.6 🎨 Renaissance
notes:
Renaissance → 'rebirth' of classical Greek and Roman culture.

Began → Italian city-states during the 1400s.

It was characterized by → intellectual creativity + artistic creativity + humanism + secularism + reason + renewed interest in classical learning.

Reasons for its emergence in Italy:
• Strategic Mediterranean location.
• Growth of trade.
• Wealthy banking and commercial cities.
• Classical Roman heritage.
• Independent city-states.
• Patronage by wealthy merchants and nobles.

Major centers → Florence + Milan + Venice + Genoa + Pisa + Siena + Rome.

Humanism → emphasized human dignity, worth, uniqueness and human reason.

Secularism → growing interest in worldly life rather than only the afterlife.

title: 4.6.1 🧠 Renaissance Humanism and Thought
notes:
Renaissance thinkers looked to ancient Greece and Rome for inspiration.

Humanists → emphasized the dignity and ability of human beings.

People increasingly used → observation + experience + reason to understand the world.

Wealthy merchants and nobles → became patrons of artists, writers and scholars.

📚 Petrarch → known as the 'Father of Humanism'; collected and studied ancient texts.

📚 Erasmus → used new methods of textual criticism and questioned aspects of Church practice.

📚 Boccaccio → wrote secular works in vernacular language.

Renaissance literature increasingly used local languages instead of Latin.

Major writers influenced by Renaissance culture → Rabelais + William Shakespeare + Cervantes.

title: 4.6.2 🖼️ Renaissance Art and Architecture
notes:
Renaissance artists aimed to make paintings and sculptures more realistic and three-dimensional.

👤 Giotto (1267–1337) → introduced greater depth, shading, emotion and realistic gestures.

👤 Masaccio (1401–1428) → developed realistic effects and use of shadows.

High Renaissance → artistic peak associated with Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Raphael.

👤 Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) → painter + sculptor + inventor + scientist.

Major works → Mona Lisa + The Last Supper.

Scientific interests → studied human anatomy through dissections; designed inventions including parachute and machine-gun-like devices.

👤 Michelangelo (1475–1564) → created David + Moses + Pietà and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

👤 Raphael → major High Renaissance painter.

🏛️ Renaissance architecture → inspired by ancient Roman columns and circular arches.

👤 Filippo Brunelleschi → designed the great dome of Florence Cathedral.

title: 4.6.3 🔬 Renaissance Science, Printing and Politics
notes:
🔭 Nicholas Copernicus → challenged the geocentric theory and proposed the heliocentric theory that Earth and planets orbit the Sun.

👤 Galileo Galilei → observations through an improved telescope supported Copernicus's ideas and challenged traditional beliefs.

🖨️ Johann Gutenberg → developed movable-type printing in Germany around 1450.

Printing press → made mass production of books possible and spread new ideas and literacy.

👤 Niccolò Machiavelli → wrote The Prince, a guide to gaining and maintaining political power.

Machiavelli → argued that rulers might need to do whatever was necessary to preserve political power.

'Reason of state' → rulers justified policies designed to strengthen and preserve the state.

Political developments → stronger taxation + professional armies + ambassadors + development of modern diplomacy.

Economic impact → increased trade + greater variety of goods + growth of cities.

title: 4.7 ✝️ The Reformation
notes:
Reformation → religious revolt against the Roman Catholic Church beginning in 1517.

Major causes:
• Renaissance spirit of inquiry.
• Criticism of Church corruption.
• Opposition to church taxes.
• Opposition to tax exemptions.
• Challenges to papal authority.
• Criticism of church teachings.
• Criticism of worldliness and nepotism.
• Sale of indulgences.

👤 Erasmus and Sir Thomas More → sought reform within the Catholic Church.

📅 1517 → Reformation became a major religious revolt.

title: 4.7.1 📜 Martin Luther and Lutheranism
notes:
👤 Martin Luther (1483–1546) → German leader of the Reformation.

He opposed → sale of indulgences and other Catholic practices.

1517 → posted the 95 Theses at Wittenberg.

Main teachings:
• Pope was not supreme authority.
• Bible was the final authority.
• Salvation came through faith in God.

1521 → Pope excommunicated Luther.

Luther → established the Lutheran Church.

He translated the New Testament into German and encouraged ordinary people to read and understand the Bible.

German princes → protected Luther and adopted Protestantism; some also seized Church lands and closed monasteries.

Lutheranism → spread to Norway, Sweden and Denmark and became official state religion there by the end of the 16th century.

title: 4.7.2 ⛪ Other Protestant Movements
notes:
👤 John Calvin (1509–1564) → major Protestant reformer based in Geneva.

Calvinism → taught predestination, the belief that those chosen by God would achieve salvation.

Calvinists → emphasized hard work and strict moral conduct.

Calvinism spread to → Switzerland + Holland + Scotland + other areas.

🏴 England → Henry VIII broke with Rome.

1534 → Act of Supremacy established an independent Church of England with the monarch as head.

👑 Elizabeth I → established a moderate form of Protestantism called Anglicanism.

Puritans → English Calvinists who opposed Anglican episcopal government and preferred Presbyterian organization.

🏴 Scotland → John Knox introduced Calvinism; Presbyterian Church became official in 1560.

🇫🇷 France → Calvinists were known as Huguenots.

title: 4.7.3 🛡️ Catholic Counter-Reformation
notes:
Counter-Reformation → Catholic response to the spread of Protestantism.

Council of Trent (1545–1563) → redefined Catholic beliefs and ended the sale of indulgences.

Catholic actions:
• Reformed some abuses.
• Banned Protestant books.
• Strengthened Church discipline.
• Established the Inquisition.

Inquisition → Church court used to investigate and punish people accused of heresy; trials could involve torture.

👤 Ignatius of Loyola → founded the Society of Jesus/Jesuits in 1534.

Jesuits → defended and spread Catholicism through missionary work.

Catholic orders → Dominicans + Franciscans + Jesuits and others worked in Africa, Asia and the Americas.

title: 4.7.4 ⚔️ Historical Significance of the Reformation
notes:
Europe became religiously divided:

✝️ Catholic south → France + Italy + Spain + Southern Germany.

✝️ Protestant north → Northern Germany + Holland + Scandinavian countries.

England → separated from Catholic Church and established Anglicanism.

Religious wars → Catholics and Protestants fought for more than a century.

Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) → religious and political conflict that killed about one-third of the German population according to the textbook.

Political impact → strengthened secular rulers and weakened papal authority.

Economic impact → reduced Church taxation in Protestant areas and encouraged some attitudes toward economic discipline, industry and commerce.

Art → Catholic art emphasized Jesus, Mary and saints; Protestant art often emphasized landscapes and secular subjects.

title: 4.8 🔬 Scientific Revolution
notes:
Scientific Revolution → period roughly 1500–1700 during which modern science began to take shape.

New approach → careful observation + experimentation + scientific reasoning.

Traditional ideas were increasingly challenged by new evidence and technology.

🔭 Astronomy became a major field of challenge.

👤 Nicholas Copernicus → heliocentric theory; Earth and other planets revolve around the Sun.

👤 Galileo Galilei → telescope observations supported heliocentrism; discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter.

1633 → Galileo was tried in Rome and confined to his home.

👤 Isaac Newton → formulated laws of motion and universal gravitation.

Universal gravitation → every object attracts every other object; attraction depends on mass and distance.

title: 4.8.1 🧪 Scientific Instruments and Discoveries
notes:
🔬 Zacharias Janssen → associated with invention of the first microscope around 1590.

👤 Anton van Leeuwenhoek → used a microscope to examine red blood cells.

👤 Evangelista Torricelli → developed the mercury barometer in 1643 for measuring atmospheric pressure.

👤 Gabriel Fahrenheit → developed a mercury thermometer in 1714.

👤 Anders Celsius → created the Celsius temperature scale in 1742.

👤 Andreas Vesalius → dissected human bodies and published detailed anatomical observations in On the Structure of the Human Body (1543).

👤 Edward Jenner → introduced vaccination against smallpox using cowpox in the late 1700s.

👤 Robert Boyle → pioneered scientific methods in chemistry and is regarded in the textbook as founder of modern chemistry.

Boyle's law → explains relationships among pressure, volume and temperature of gases.

title: 4.8.2 💡 Enlightenment — Age of Reason
notes:
Enlightenment → intellectual movement that applied reason and critical thinking to government, religion, economics, education and society.

Reached its height → mid-1700s.

Also called → Age of Reason.

📍 France → major center of Enlightenment thought.

Philosophes → French intellectuals who promoted reason and social criticism.

Five core ideas:

1️⃣ Reason → truth can be discovered through logical thinking.
2️⃣ Nature → what is natural is good and reasonable.
3️⃣ Happiness → people should seek well-being in earthly life.
4️⃣ Progress → society and humanity can improve.
5️⃣ Liberty → individuals should enjoy greater freedom.

title: 4.8.3 🧠 Enlightenment Philosophers and Ideas
notes:
👤 John Locke (1632–1704) → natural rights: life + liberty + property.

👤 Montesquieu (1689–1755) → separation of powers.

👤 Voltaire (1694–1778) → freedom of thought + freedom of expression + religious freedom.

👤 Denis Diderot (1717–1784) → major French Enlightenment thinker and encyclopedist.

👤 Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) → major Enlightenment philosopher concerned with political and social ideas.

👤 Cesare Beccaria → opposed torture and supported reform of criminal justice.

👤 Mary Wollstonecraft → advocated women's equality.

📌 Enlightenment ideas later influenced political constitutions, rights movements, religious freedom and challenges to absolute authority.

title: 🏆 UNIT 4 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
🏰 EUROPEAN MIDDLE AGES
476 A.D. → fall of Western Roman Empire.

Byzantine → Eastern Roman Empire; survived about 1,000 years after Western Rome.

Justinian I → greatest Byzantine expansion.

Justinian Code → Roman law collection.

Theodora → Justinian's wife, advisor and co-ruler.

1453 → Ottoman conquest of Constantinople ended Byzantine Empire.

⚔️ WESTERN EUROPE
Germanic kingdoms → Ostrogoths + Visigoths + Franks + Burgundians + Saxons.

Charles Martel → Battle of Tours, 732.

Charlemagne → reunited much of Western Europe; crowned emperor in 800.

🌾 FEUDALISM
King → Lords → Vassals → Knights → Peasants/Serfs.

Manor → center of rural economy.

Demesne → lord's direct land.

Vassalage → land in exchange for loyalty/service.

Chivalry → knightly code of conduct.


🏘️ TOWNS AND TRADE

11th century → revival of trade and towns.

Guilds → merchant and craft organizations.

Middle class → merchants + traders + artisans.

Universities → developed during the 1100s.

✝️ CRUSADES
1096–1270 → major Crusades.

1099 → First Crusade captured Jerusalem.

1187 → Saladin recaptured Jerusalem.

1204 → Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople.

Effects → increased trade + navigation + money economy + weakened serfdom + wider contacts.

☪️ ISLAM
610 → Muhammad began preaching.

622 → Hijra to Medina.

630 → Muhammad entered Mecca.

632 → Muhammad died.

Caliphs → Abu Bakr + Umar + Uthman + Ali.

Sunni → caliphate and Sunna.

Shi'a → Imamate and Ali's succession.

Kharijites → independent sect emphasizing qualified leadership.

Umayyad → 661–750, Damascus.

Abbasid → 750–1258, Baghdad.

1258 → Mongols destroyed Baghdad.

🧠 MUSLIM CIVILIZATION

Golden Age → 800–1200.

Achievements → mathematics + astronomy + medicine + chemistry + geography + history + agriculture + trade + architecture + literature.

Ibn Sina → Canon on Medicine.

Ibn Khaldun → scientific study of history; emphasized social/economic causes.


🕌 OTTOMANS

Osman I → founder.

1453 → Mehmet II captured Constantinople.

Istanbul → Ottoman capital.

Suleiman I → height of Ottoman power.

Janissaries → elite infantry.

Sipahi → cavalry.

Timar → military landholding/fief.

Millet → religious community system.

🇨🇳 CHINA

Mandate of Heaven → divine right to rule.

Dynastic Cycle → rise → prosperity → corruption → loss of mandate → collapse → new dynasty.


Sui → reunified China + Grand Canal.

Tang → 618–907 + prosperity + culture.

Song → 960–1279 + commerce + gunpowder + compass + movable printing.

Yuan → Mongol rule under Kublai Khan.

Ming → 1368–1644 + stability + naval expeditions.

Qing → 1644–1912.

💰 EARLY CAPITALISM

Trade + towns + guilds + craft production + banks + bourgeoisie + long-distance trade → growth of capitalist relations.


🏦 Italian cities → Venice + Genoa became major commercial centers.

🧭 AGE OF EXPLORATION

Portugal + Spain → leading explorers in 15th–16th centuries.

Henry the Navigator → encouraged Portuguese exploration.

Vasco da Gama → reached India around Africa, 1497–98.

Columbus → reached Americas, 1492.
Magellan expedition → first circumnavigation, 1519–22.

🌽 COLUMBIAN EXCHANGE
Old World ↔ New World exchange of crops, animals and diseases.

🎨 RENAISSANCE
Meaning → rebirth.
Origin → Italy, 1400s.
Humanism → human dignity + reason.
Leonardo → Mona Lisa + Last Supper.
Michelangelo → David + Sistine Chapel.
Brunelleschi → Florence Cathedral dome.
Gutenberg → movable-type printing.
Machiavelli → The Prince.

✝️ REFORMATION
1517 → Martin Luther + 95 Theses.
Lutheranism → justification by faith + Bible as final authority.
Calvinism → predestination.
Henry VIII → Act of Supremacy, 1534.
Elizabeth I → Anglicanism.
Council of Trent → Catholic Counter-Reformation.
Jesuits → Ignatius of Loyola.

🔬 SCIENTIFIC REVOLUTION
c.1500–1700.
Copernicus → heliocentric theory.
Galileo → telescope observations.
Newton → universal gravitation.
Vesalius → anatomy.
Boyle → modern chemistry/scientific method.
Jenner → smallpox vaccination.

💡 ENLIGHTENMENT
Age of Reason → reason + nature + happiness + progress + liberty.
Locke → natural rights.
Montesquieu → separation of powers.
Voltaire → freedom of thought/expression/religion.
Beccaria → against torture.
Wollstonecraft → women's equality.
